> On Jul 7, 2015, at 10:08 AM, Shravan Vasishth <vasishth...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Hi Bob,
>
> I saw your HMC demo in your Australia talk. Is it possible to get the code for that, or is it too cumbersome to share? I guess it must be quite involved since you showed gifs.


I just responded to the list on this one:

https://www.dropbox.com/sh/vobwxzt256l53jl/AAC6-ho_ESw37aNESkQlKvZHa?dl=0

> Very nice talk by the way.

Thanks. It went awfully fast!

I just ran into Kyle Mahowald, a student of Ted Gibson at MIT, who was
telling me how much he liked your tutorial on Stan for psycholinguistics!
He was interested in getting involved, but thought you'd pretty much
covered all the bases that a psycholinguist would need.

> I still can't understand where the Jacobian is in the LJK Cholesky factorization;
> is there an introductory book or article I can read that explains this to non-mathematicians like me?

It was Greek to me, too, when Ben first wrote it down. But
once you get your head around the fact that determinants are
calculate volume, the rest is easy. Think about an axis-aligned hyperrectangle,
represented as a diagonal matrix --- its volume is the
product of the diagonal entries, and the volume's invariant to
rotation off axis alignment.

> I know what a Jacobian is and what it's for, I just don't see where it comes in here. I understand that the Cholesky factorization takes a sort of square root, so that's a kind of transformation like
>
> Y = \sqrt{X}
>
> So, this is the classic situation where a change of variables will need a Jacobian term. I can write all that down analytically for the textbook examples. But I don't know how to proceed with the Jacobian involved in the Cholesky factor.

The Jacobian is calculated for the inverse function from unconstrained
to constrained. It first creates a lower-triangular L and then
maps to L * L'.

There's a chapter near the end of the manual that goes over all the
Jacobians in gory detail, starting with the general definitions
of Jacobians.

The tricky bit of the Cholesky is generating an appropriate
L such that L * L' is a correlation matrix --- each row
of L is of Euclidean length 1 and must have a positive diagonal entry.
Then there's the algebra to reduce the Jacobian.

I still find the LKJ paper hard going, but that goes over several
alternative ways to do it --- the decomposition to unconstrained
parameters we use isn't the only one possible.

- Bob

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: your talk in Australia
parts:
On Tuesday, July 7, 2015 at 10:53:33 AM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>  I still can't understand where the Jacobian is in the LJK Cholesky factorization;
> is there an introductory book or article I can read that explains this to non-mathematicians like me?

No, there isn't. Part of the problem is that there are actually 4 Jacobians. If Lambda is a correlation matrix of order K, the LKJ (2009) paper derives a PDF
f(Lambda | eta) \ propto det(Lambda)^(eta - 1)
It is more useful numerically to work with a Cholesky factor of a correlation matrix L, such that Lambda = L * L'. In that case, you have the new PDF via the change-of-variables theorem
f(L | eta) \propto det(J) * det(L * L')^(eta - 1) = det(J) * det(L)^(2 * eta - 2)
The Jacobian matrix, J, for the transformation from L to Lambda is not so bad (it only involves the diagonal elements of L) and is described at the end of the Stan User Manual. Although this transformation is straightforward, the LKJ (2009) paper did not actually work this PDF out. To compound matters, the LKJ (2009) paper shows an equivalence in distribution to something an earlier paper called the "onion method" of generating a random correlation matrix that would have been much simpler if they had just derived f(L | eta).

What the LKJ (2009) paper did do is derive a transformation from K * (K - 1) / 2 partial correlations to K * (K - 1) / 2 Pearson correlations (that fill a triangle of Lambda). What Stan actually does is a transformation from the (K * (K - 1) / 2 lower-triangular elements of L to the K * (K - 1) / 2 partial correlations. This part is potentially confusing because there are actually many different ways of defining a set of  K * (K - 1) / 2 partial correlations, depending on what gets partialed out. However, from a numerical perspective, the choice is obvious because only one partialization scheme avoids having to invert submatrices, which is what LKJ calls "partial correlations on a C-vine" or what I call "canonical partial correlations". A canonical partial correlation between variables i and j is the correlation in the residuals of i and the residuals of j when i and j are each regressed on all variables (if any) before the i-th where i < j. So, Stan only utilizes canonical partial correlations, which are proportional to the lower-triangular elements of L, in which case the Jacobian matrix for this transformation is diagonal.

In any event, the LKJ (2009) paper works out the transformation from canonical partial correlations to the lower-triangular elements of Lambda without going through L. It turns out that if the canonical partial correlations have independent symmetric Beta priors on the (-1,1) interval, then the PDF for Lambda given above follows. Anyway, whether you go through L or not, you have these canonical partial correlations that are constrained to the (-1,1) interval but Stan needs parameters over the whole real number line. So, we do a Fisher (inverse) transformation of each canonical partial correlation to the real line, which is pretty simple and described in the Stan manual.

So there you have it. That said, none of these transformations give much statistical insight. I don't know why you would believe that the canonical partial correlations have these particular Beta prior distributions, except that they imply a simple form for f(Lambda | eta) \proto det(Lambda)^(eta - 1) which is easy to make uniform by setting eta = 1 and easy to make the identity matrix the mode by setting eta > 1. And the only reasons --- although they are substantial --- to work with L rather than Lambda is numeric stability and computational speed.

Ben

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: your talk in Australia
parts:
At a high level, here's the drill.

Suppose Sigma is a correlation matrix and nu > 0, with

p(Sigma | nu) = LKJ(Sigma | nu);

Then the density of its Cholesky factor

L = chol(Sigma)

is given by

p(L | nu) = LKJ(L * L' | nu) * | det(J_f) |

where J_f is the Jacobian of the function

f(L) = (L * L').

Note that f is the inverse of the Cholesky factorization.

Then it's just a matter of being a lot better than me
at turning the crank on the determinant and derivative
calcluations :-).

- Bob
